summary: The Sealion 5 is BYD's cheapest plug-in hybrid at $33,990 before on-roads for the Essential, a front-drive medium SUV that undercuts the Sealion 6 by $9,000 while matching or beating it on boot space. Australian reviewers agree the value case is strong and that ride comfort and rear-seat room are better than the price suggests, but they split on the cabin and driving experience, with several calling the steering vague and the 1.5-litre engine noisy once the battery is flat. The firm reservations are the three-star ANCAP rating awarded in September 2026 (the first BYD to miss five stars), 3.3kW AC-only charging, and how quickly running costs climb without home charging.
pros: At $33,990 before on-road costs the Essential is the cheapest plug-in hybrid held here, undercutting the Geely Starray EM-i Complete by $3,500 and BYD's own Sealion 6 Essential by $9,000
463-litre boot with the seats up (1,410 litres folded) is larger than the physically bigger Sealion 6's 425 litres, so the battery packaging costs less practicality than usual in the class

Premium's 18.3kWh battery is rated at 85km of WLTP electric range in the UK (100km on the NEDC figure BYD Australia quotes), enough for a typical Melbourne commuter to run several days between charges without starting the engine
High-voltage battery is covered for 8 years/160,000km, two years beyond the 6-year/150,000km unconditional vehicle warranty
CarsGuide says the cabin punches above its price and CarExpert calls it intuitive, while Chasing Cars rates rear-seat room as genuinely adult-sized
cons: Three-star ANCAP rating (September 2026, both grades): Crash Avoidance scored 51% and Safe Driving 48%, lane-keeping failed the road-edge test, and it lacks child presence detection and eCall, where the Sealion 6 carries five stars

Charge-sustaining fuel use is the number that matters: BYD quotes 4.5L/100km (Essential) and 4.6L/100km (Premium) with the battery below 25 per cent against a 1.2-1.3L/100km label, and Chasing Cars recorded 8.1L/100km on country roads, so a buyer who cannot charge at home loses most of the reason to own it
3.3kW AC onboard charger and no DC fast-charging at all: CarsGuide estimates 4-5 hours from low on the Essential, so an away-from-home top-up is effectively impossible
Front-wheel drive only, rated to tow just 750kg braked, and supplied with a tyre repair kit rather than a spare wheel

Reviewers criticise the steering as light or vague and the engine as noisy once the battery is depleted; CarsGuide also notes limited steering-column adjustment and some high-speed unsettledness, and Chasing Cars calls the cabin plastics cheap
